source.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
source.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
source.date_note: AI RMF 1.0 was published 2023-01-26. NIST states in 2026 that AI RMF 1.0 is being revised; this case analyzes the stable 1.0 framework and records the revision as a living follow-up rather than silently treating 1.0 as final.

inspection.method: Direct inspection of the official AI RMF 1.0 publication/PDF, the NIST AI RMF Core pages, and the official Playbook/Manage material for operating-model and non-checklist boundaries.
gaps: This case does not enumerate every category/subcategory or every trustworthy-AI characteristic in depth.
The 2026 revision of AI RMF 1.0 is in progress; revised framework semantics should be treated as a future re-analysis event.

prior_knowledge.query: Understand the AI RMF operating model, its core functions and how risk management should shape practical AI system decisions; distinguish framework guidance from specific technical controls.

content_map.problem: Organizations need a practical way to reason about AI risks across technical, organizational and societal context without assuming one sector, one use case or one fixed list of controls.
content_map.thesis: AI RMF 1.0 provides a voluntary, context-sensitive operating framework built around four functions—GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE—where governance is cross-cutting and the other functions are iterated and tailored rather than executed as a mandatory checklist.
sections: Part 1: Framing Risk and trustworthy AI characteristics
mechanisms: GOVERN establishes policies, accountability, culture, roles and risk-tolerance structures that inform all other functions.
MAP recognizes the system context, intended purpose, affected actors and risks arising from that context.
MEASURE selects and applies qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods to assess, benchmark and monitor mapped risks and trustworthiness characteristics.
MANAGE prioritizes assessed risks, chooses responses, allocates resources and can produce explicit go/no-go or continue/decommission decisions.
Functions are continuously cross-referenced across the AI lifecycle rather than treated as a one-pass ordered workflow.
examples: An organization maps who could be affected by an AI decision and the intended deployment context before choosing which fairness or performance measurements matter.
A measured risk can be accepted, mitigated, transferred or cause a deployment not to proceed depending on impact, likelihood, risk tolerance and available responses.
Governance defines who owns AI risk decisions and documentation instead of leaving risk assessment as an isolated model-testing activity.
claims: AI RMF 1.0 is voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific and use-case agnostic.
The Core contains GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE and MANAGE, and GOVERN is designed as a cross-cutting function.
The functions are not a checklist or necessarily an ordered series of steps; risk management is continuous and iterative across the AI lifecycle.
MAP builds contextual knowledge and identifies risks related to that context.
MEASURE assesses and monitors identified risks using appropriate qualitative, quantitative or mixed methods.
MANAGE prioritizes and responds to risks and includes decisions about whether development or deployment should proceed.
The Playbook offers optional suggested actions and does not turn the framework into a universal technical-control catalog.
evidence: NIST AI 100-1 publication metadata and abstract establish the 2023 release, voluntary scope and intended audience.
AI RMF 1.0 §5 and Figure 5 define the four functions and the cross-cutting governance model.
AIRC Core reproduces the framework's statement that actions are not a checklist and functions can be applied iteratively in context.
NIST Playbook states its suggestions are voluntary and neither a checklist nor a complete ordered process.
assumptions: Organizations tailor categories, subcategories, measurements and responses to their own context and risk tolerance.
Risk management involves multidisciplinary and potentially external perspectives rather than only model engineering.
Specific technical controls, tests and metrics must be selected separately to achieve the framework outcomes.
limitations: AI RMF is a voluntary framework and does not replace binding legal, regulatory, contractual or sector-specific obligations.
The framework defines outcomes and categories but does not prescribe one universal set of technical controls or metrics for every AI system.
The four functions should not be implemented as a rigid waterfall sequence; governance is cross-cutting and the process is iterative.
A framework-compliant process does not by itself prove that a deployed AI system is trustworthy or that residual risks are acceptable.
AI RMF 1.0 is being revised in 2026, so future framework changes require explicit re-analysis rather than silent reinterpretation.
open_questions: Which technical control/evaluation catalogs best operationalize specific AI RMF outcomes for a concrete enterprise AI system?
How will the forthcoming revision change the 1.0 Core, trustworthiness characteristics or profile model?

selection.requested_focus: Understand the AI RMF operating model, its core functions and how risk management should shape practical AI system decisions; distinguish framework guidance from specific technical controls.
coherent_core: GOVERN is the cross-cutting organizational risk-management substrate.
MAP establishes context and identifies risks that matter in that context.
MEASURE turns mapped risks into evidence through assessment, testing and monitoring.
MANAGE prioritizes risks and chooses responses, including go/no-go decisions.
The functions are iterative outcomes, not a mandatory four-step checklist or a ready-made controls catalog.
prerequisites: difference between framework outcomes and implementation controls
drop_notes: Do not expand every AI RMF category/subcategory into a long compliance checklist in this first mental model.
Do not infer that one technical control automatically satisfies an entire function or trustworthiness characteristic.
Do not treat the 2026 revision-in-progress as evidence that AI RMF 1.0 outcomes have already changed.
connections: Controlled execution, policy-as-code and observability may become implementation controls inside an AI risk program, but AI RMF itself does not assert those project-specific architectures.
The framework is a decision/governance layer over many possible AI technologies rather than a model architecture or agent runtime.

verification_candidates.question: What concrete changes will NIST make in the revised AI RMF after the 2026 revision process?
verification_candidates.reason: The current NIST site explicitly says AI RMF 1.0 is being revised.

verification_candidates.question: Which AI RMF profiles or sector frameworks best map to enterprise AI-agent deployments?
verification_candidates.reason: Profiles are the bridge from use-case-agnostic outcomes to context-specific practice.
